result:
Language is full of fossils. We still "dial" phone numbers, though almost no one alive under thirty has turned a rotary dial. We "hang up" on calls that end with a tap on glass. We shoot "footage" on devices that contain no film, measured in no feet. We "roll down" car windows by pressing a button, and we save documents by clicking a tiny picture of a floppy disk that many users have never held.

I love these leftovers. They're proof that when the world changes, words mostly get reassigned rather than replaced. The object disappears and the word stays behind, like a shell after the animal has gone, and eventually something new moves in.

Go back further and the fossils get stranger. A "deadline" was once a literal line around a Civil War prison camp; cross it and guards would shoot. "Clue" comes from "clew," a ball of thread, the kind Theseus unspooled through the labyrinth. To have a clue was to have something to follow out of the dark. A "disaster" is a bad star, a leftover from the days when we blamed the sky for our troubles.

You can say "disaster" without knowing any astrology. Still, I find it comforting. Every sentence we speak is built from parts handed down by people who were solving entirely different problems: navigating mazes, guarding prisoners, reading the heavens. We're all speaking in hand-me-downs, and they fit surprisingly well.

Someday "swipe" will puzzle someone too. I hope they look it up.
